title: The Resurrection and the Life: Lazarus Raised
summary: Jesus hears that his friend Lazarus is sick but waits two days, and by the time he reaches Bethany Lazarus has been dead four days. He tells Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life,” weeps with Mary and the mourners, and calls Lazarus out of the tomb. The sign leads many to believe, but it also drives the council under the high priest Caiaphas to plan Jesus' death, and Caiaphas unknowingly prophesies that one man will die for the people.
story:
This is the last and greatest of the signs in the first half of John (the seventh, for readers who count the walking on the sea among them), and it is the hinge of the Gospel. Every earlier sign pointed to Jesus as the giver of life; this one shows him defeating death itself. It is also the event that directly causes his arrest. In the other Gospels the cleansing of the temple is the last straw for the authorities; in John, the decision to kill Jesus follows the raising of Lazarus. So the chapter makes a painful exchange plain: Jesus gives life to Lazarus, and it costs him his own.

The chapter picks up where chapter 10 left off. Jesus has withdrawn across the Jordan after an attempt to stone him (10:31, 10:39-40), and the disciples know that going back to Judea means danger (verse 8). Chapter 5 had already announced that the hour was coming when the dead would hear the voice of the Son of God and live (5:25-29); here that promise is acted out at one tomb. The chapter also gathers threads from earlier: the blind man healed in chapter 9 (verse 37), the shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep and gathers the scattered into one flock (10:11, 10:16, compare verses 50 to 52), and the glory of God revealed in the signs (2:11, compare verses 4 and 40). From here the story moves toward the final Passover, which is near (verse 55). Chapter 12 opens with a dinner in Bethany where Lazarus sits at the table and Mary anoints Jesus for burial.
historical:
Bethany was a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem (verse 18), a little under two miles, on the road down to Jericho. The modern Arab town there is called al-Eizariya, a name that preserves the Greek Lazarion, the place of Lazarus. Eusebius's Onomasticon, written in the early fourth century, says the place of Lazarus was still pointed out at Bethany, and the pilgrim Egeria, in Jerusalem around 381 to 384, describes the whole church going out to the Lazarium on the Saturday before Palm Sunday (Itinerarium 29). Going to Bethany meant returning to Judea, where Jesus had just escaped stoning (10:31), which is why Thomas expects to die with him (verse 16). The other Gospels know Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38-42) and place a supper and an anointing at Bethany in Jesus' last week (Mark 14:3-9).

The council (synedrion, verse 47), usually called the Sanhedrin, was the Jewish high council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders, and scribes, including some Pharisees, and presided over by the high priest. Under Roman rule it governed internal Jewish affairs, but it held its authority at Rome's pleasure. Caiaphas, called high priest “that year” (verses 49 and 51), was appointed by the Roman prefect Valerius Gratus around AD 18 and removed by the Syrian legate Vitellius around AD 36 or 37 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.35 and 18.95), an unusually long tenure that suggests he worked well with the Roman governors, including Pontius Pilate. John 18:13 says he was the son-in-law of Annas, the former high priest. John's phrase most likely means high priest in that fateful year, the year of Jesus' death. In December 1990 a family tomb was found in the Peace Forest south of Jerusalem's Old City containing an ornate ossuary (a limestone box for bones) inscribed Yehosef bar Qayafa, Joseph son of Caiaphas, with the bones of several people, among them a man of about sixty. Josephus gives the high priest's personal name as Joseph (Antiquities 18.35), and many scholars think the box belonged to his family, though some doubt the identification.

The council's fear was realistic. Rome did not tolerate popular movements around a would-be king, and Josephus records several that ended in slaughter. The leaders worried that a crowd following Jesus would bring the legions and cost them their place, meaning the temple (compare 2 Maccabees 5:19 and Acts 6:13-14), and their nation (verse 48). The irony is sharp for John's readers: Rome did destroy the temple in AD 70. Caiaphas's words were taken by John as prophecy because of his office. The high priest had once carried the Urim and Thummim for learning God's will (Exodus 28:30, Numbers 27:21), and Josephus says the high priest John Hyrcanus was granted the gift of prophecy (Antiquities 13.299).

After the council's decision, Jesus withdrew to a town called Ephraim near the wilderness (verse 54). It is usually identified with et-Taiyibeh, a hill town north of Jerusalem near Bethel overlooking the wilderness and the Jordan valley, probably the Ophrah of Joshua 18:23 and the Ephron of 2 Chronicles 13:19; Josephus mentions a small town of Ephraim near Bethel taken by Vespasian during the war with Rome (Jewish War 4.551). The pilgrims who came up early to purify themselves before Passover (verse 55) were following the law that anyone unclean, for example through contact with a corpse, must be purified before eating the Passover (Numbers 9:6-12, 19:11-12; 2 Chronicles 30:17-18).

As elsewhere, the Jews in the chapter are a varied group. Many come to comfort the sisters, many believe (verse 45), and some report to the Pharisees; the plot is the work of the council, not a people.
cultural:
Jewish burial happened quickly, usually on the day of death (compare Acts 5:6-10), since bodies decayed fast in the heat. The body was washed (Acts 9:37), wrapped in linen strips with spices (John 19:39-40), and laid in a family tomb. Around Jerusalem these were caves cut into the soft limestone, with a low entrance, a central chamber, and burial niches or benches; after a year the bones might be gathered into an ossuary. The entrance was closed with a stone. Amos Kloner, surveying more than nine hundred Second Temple tombs around Jerusalem, found that nearly all were closed with square blocking stones and only four, belonging to wealthy families, with round rolling stones (Biblical Archaeology Review, 1999). John's words in verse 38, a cave with a stone laid across or upon it, fit either kind. The grave clothes of verse 44 are keiriai, bands or strips, and a soudarion, a cloth for the face (from the Latin sudarium, a sweat cloth), the same word used of the cloth in Jesus' tomb (20:7).

Mourning was public and communal. The first seven days were the most intense (Genesis 50:10; Sirach 22:12 says mourning for the dead lasts seven days), and friends and neighbors were expected to come and sit with the family; this is why many Jews from Jerusalem are in the house (verses 19 and 31). The mourners' loud wailing (klaiō, verse 33) was customary, and professional mourners and flute players were hired where families could afford them; the Mishnah says even the poorest man in Israel should provide at least two flutes and one wailing woman at his wife's funeral (m. Ketubbot 4:4; compare Matthew 9:23). Mary's staying seated in the house (verse 20) fits the custom of mourners sitting to receive visitors, and those who follow her assume she has gone to weep at the tomb (verse 31).

The detail that Lazarus had been dead four days matters. Later rabbinic writings record the belief that for three days the soul hovers near the body, hoping to return, and departs when it sees the face begin to change (Leviticus Rabbah 18:1; Genesis Rabbah 100:7). Whatever John's readers believed, four days meant that death was beyond doubt, and Martha's blunt warning about the smell (verse 39) makes the same point.

Martha's confession that her brother will rise “in the resurrection at the last day” (verse 24) reflects the belief of the Pharisees and many ordinary Jews that God would raise the dead at the end of the age (Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7:9, 7:14). The second benediction of the Amidah, the synagogue's central prayer, praises God who gives life to the dead, and the Mishnah denies a share in the world to come to anyone who says there is no resurrection of the dead (m. Sanhedrin 10:1). The Sadducees, the party of many chief priests, denied it (Mark 12:18, Acts 23:8; Josephus, Antiquities 18.16). Jesus doesn't correct Martha's hope but draws it into himself: the resurrection is not only an event at the end but a person present now. The names in the family were ordinary ones. Lazarus is a Greek form of Eleazar, ‘God has helped’, and Tal Ilan's Lexicon of Jewish Names in Late Antiquity (2002) shows Eleazar, Mary, and Martha among the most common names of Jewish Palestine in this period.
literary:
The chapter is carefully paced. The message from the sisters is gentle, stating the need without making a request (verse 3). The delay (verse 6) builds tension, and a sequence of encounters follows: with the disciples (verses 7 to 16), with Martha (verses 17 to 27), with Mary and the mourners (verses 28 to 37), and at the tomb (verses 38 to 44). Each encounter turns on a misunderstanding or a partial understanding. The disciples take sleep literally (verses 11 to 13), a characteristic Johannine misunderstanding, and Thomas's courage (verse 16) is real but does not yet see what Jesus is going to do. Martha believes that God will give Jesus whatever he asks (verse 22) and believes in the resurrection at the last day (verse 24), but she does not expect what happens at the tomb (verse 39). Martha and Mary greet Jesus with the same words, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died” (verses 21 and 32), but Jesus answers each differently: Martha with teaching and a question, Mary with tears. The saying about twelve hours of daylight (verses 9 and 10) echoes 9:4-5 and places the trip under the light of the Father's appointed time.

The fifth of the seven ‘I am’ sayings with an image, “I am the resurrection and the life” (verse 25), stands at the center. It is followed by two balanced promises, one for those who die (they will live) and one for those who live (they will never die), and by Martha's confession, the fullest in the Gospel before Thomas's (20:28) and close in wording to the purpose statement of the whole book (20:31). The raising itself is told in a few lines: a command about the stone, a prayer, a loud voice, and a man coming out still bound. Jesus' prayer (verses 41 and 42) is thanksgiving spoken aloud for the sake of the crowd, a public sign that the work is the Father's.

The chapter's second half is built on irony. The council fears that if they do nothing, everyone will believe and Rome will destroy them (verse 48); they act, and Rome destroys the temple anyway. Caiaphas means that it is politically expedient for one man to die instead of the nation; John tells the reader that he spoke more truly than he knew, and extends the prophecy beyond the nation to the scattered children of God (verses 51 and 52), which takes up the other sheep and one flock of 10:16. The chapter is also full of anticipations. Verse 2 speaks of Mary's anointing before it happens (12:3), the stone at the tomb and the grave clothes point ahead to Jesus' own tomb (20:1, 20:5-7), and the chapter ends with the crowds asking whether Jesus will come to the feast (verse 56), the last Passover.

outline.t: News of Lazarus' illness and the deliberate delay
Martha: I am the resurrection and the life
Mary and the mourners; Jesus weeps
The council plots, and Caiaphas prophesies
Jesus withdraws as Passover draws near

doctrines.note: Jesus does not only promise the resurrection at the last day; he says, “I am the resurrection and the life” (verse 25). Lazarus was raised to die again, so his raising is a sign rather than the thing itself. It points to Jesus' own bodily resurrection a few days later, which begins the final resurrection of all his people.

The same chapter shows Jesus deeply moved, troubled, and weeping at a friend's grave (verses 33 to 35) and calling a four-day-dead man out by a word (verse 43). Leo the Great's Tome (449), read at the Council of Chalcedon, used this very contrast to show that the one Christ is truly human and truly divine.

Faith is the chapter's aim. Jesus is glad for the disciples' sake, so that they may believe (verse 15); he asks Martha, “Do you believe this?” (verse 26); he tells her that if she believed she would see the glory of God (verse 40); he prays so that the crowd may believe (verse 42); and many do (verse 45). Martha's confession in verse 27 is the faith John wrote his Gospel to produce (20:31).

Caiaphas says it is better that one man die for the people (verse 50). John sees in the cynical calculation a true prophecy: Jesus would die for the nation and for the scattered children of God, to gather them into one (verses 51 and 52). The preposition for (huper) marks a death on behalf of others.

Jesus knows he will raise Lazarus, yet he weeps (verse 35) and is deeply moved. Grief is not unbelief, and the delay that caused the sisters' grief was not indifference (verses 5 and 6). The Son of God enters human sorrow and stands with those who mourn before he acts.

words.note: Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. It occurs about forty-two times in the New Testament and four times in John (5:29 twice, 11:24, 11:25). Martha uses it of the general resurrection at the last day, and Jesus takes the same word as a name for himself. In the New Testament it means bodily resurrection, not the survival of the soul alone, and BDAG treats its use here as the resurrection of the dead at the end, embodied in a person.

Embrimaomai, to be deeply moved, used in verses 33 and 38. It occurs five times in the New Testament: twice here, once in Mark 14:5 of the bystanders scolding the woman who anointed Jesus, and in Matthew 9:30 and Mark 1:43 of Jesus sternly warning people he had healed. Outside the Bible it can describe the snorting of a horse, and lexicons give senses of indignation and stern rebuke. Many interpreters think it here expresses anger as well as sorrow: B. B. Warfield (The Emotional Life of Our Lord, 1912) argued that Jesus was enraged at death, the enemy that destroys God's creation, while others see indignation at the unbelief around him, and still others read it as overwhelming emotion. Coupled with in spirit, it keeps Jesus' response from being merely sentimental.

Tarassō, to stir up, trouble, disturb. It occurs about seventeen times in the New Testament and six times in John: the stirred water at Bethesda (5:7), Jesus troubled here (verse 33), in the face of his hour (12:27), and at the betrayal (13:21), and the disciples told not to let their hearts be troubled (14:1, 14:27). Jesus is troubled in the same way he will later tell his disciples not to be, because he has entered the trouble first.

Dakruō, to weep or shed tears. It occurs only here in the New Testament (verse 35). It differs from klaiō, the loud wailing of Mary and the mourners (verse 33), and suggests quiet tears rather than public lament. The shortest verse in most English Bibles carries great weight: the one who is the resurrection weeps at a grave.

Koimaō, to sleep, fall asleep. It occurs about eighteen times in the New Testament, most often as a gentle word for the death of believers (Acts 7:60, 1 Corinthians 15:20, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-15). The disciples take it literally (verses 12 and 13), and Jesus has to say plainly, Lazarus is dead. For Jesus death is a sleep because he can wake the sleeper, which is the Christian use of the word in a nutshell.

Phileō, to love as a friend, to have affection for. It occurs about twenty-five times in the New Testament and thirteen times in John. The sisters' message speaks of the one you love (phileō, verse 3), the narrator says Jesus loved them (agapaō, verse 5), and the bystanders say see how he loved him (phileō, verse 36). John uses the two verbs interchangeably here, a caution against building too much on the difference between them elsewhere (21:15-17). Lazarus is also called our friend (philos, verse 11).

Sumpherō, to be advantageous, profitable, better. It occurs about fifteen times in the New Testament and three times in John (11:50, 16:7, 18:14). Caiaphas argues from expediency: it is better for you that one man die. John recalls the saying at the trial (18:14), and Jesus uses the same verb when he tells the disciples it is better for them that he go away so the Spirit may come (16:7). The same death that Caiaphas calls politically useful is, in God's purpose, the greatest good for the world.

Prophēteuō, to prophesy, speak under divine inspiration. It occurs about twenty-eight times in the New Testament and only here in John (verse 51). John does not say Caiaphas was a prophet in character or intention; he says that as high priest that year he spoke words whose true meaning came from God. Like Balaam (Numbers 23 and 24), an unwilling mouth can speak God's word.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as Lord over death. The prophets had promised that God would open graves and bring his people out (Ezekiel 37:12-13), that the dead would rise (Isaiah 26:19, Daniel 12:2), and that God would swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:8). Elijah and Elisha had raised dead boys after lying on them and praying (1 Kings 17:17-24, 2 Kings 4:32-37), but Jesus gives thanks that he has already been heard and then speaks a command, calling a dead man out by name, as he said in 5:28 that all in their graves would hear his voice. At the same time, the chapter shows his full humanity: he loves his friends, he is troubled, and he weeps. John sets the two together deliberately, and the church's confession that Christ is truly God and truly human finds some of its clearest ground here.

Above all, the chapter points ahead. The one who raises Lazarus is about to die so that others may live, and the council's decision is taken because of this very sign. Caiaphas's words, one man dying for the people, state the heart of the gospel from the lips of an enemy, and John widens them to the gathering of the scattered children of God (verse 52), a hope rooted in the prophets' promises to gather the scattered people (Isaiah 11:12, Jeremiah 31:10, Ezekiel 34:12). Lazarus comes out bound in grave clothes and must be unwrapped by others; Jesus' own grave clothes will be left lying in the tomb, the face cloth folded apart (20:5-7), because he rises never to die again. Hebrews says that through death Jesus destroyed the one who has the power of death and freed those held in slavery by fear of it (Hebrews 2:14-15). Martha's confession, that he is the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world (verse 27), is exactly what John wrote his book so that readers would believe (20:31).
interpretation:
The raising of Lazarus was the most frequently painted miracle in early Christian funerary art. In the Roman catacombs from the third century onward, Christ is shown touching with a staff a small tomb-house in which Lazarus stands wrapped like a mummy, a picture of the resurrection hope of those buried there. The fathers used the story as proof of the resurrection of the body and of Christ's two natures. John Chrysostom's homilies on John (62 to 64, around 390) dwell on Jesus' tears and his prayer. Augustine's Tractates on John 49 read the three raisings in the Gospels as degrees of spiritual death: Jairus's daughter, dead inside the house, as sin in the heart; the widow's son, carried out, as sin in the deed; and Lazarus, four days in the tomb, as sin hardened into habit, from which Christ can still raise a person, while the church is told to unbind him. Pope Leo the Great's Tome (449), which the Council of Chalcedon (451) received, used the contrast between weeping for a dead friend and calling him out of a four-day grave as its example of the two natures in one person.

The church's calendar kept the story before Easter. Egeria describes Jerusalem Christians going out to the Lazarium on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, and the Orthodox churches still keep Lazarus Saturday on that day, linking the raising to the entry into Jerusalem that follows in John 12. In the West, John 11 belonged to the Lenten preparation of candidates for baptism; the Roman Catholic rite of adult initiation and the Revised Common Lectionary read verses 1 to 45 on the fifth Sunday of Lent in Year A. Medieval legend sent Lazarus and his sisters to Provence, and a separate Eastern tradition made him bishop of Kition in Cyprus, where the church of Saint Lazarus in Larnaca claims his tomb. Calvin's commentary (1553) stressed that Christ's delay tested and trained faith, and B. B. Warfield's essay The Emotional Life of Our Lord (1912) made verse 33 the classic text for Jesus' anger at death.

Painters found in the chapter one of their great subjects. Giotto painted it in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua (about 1305). Sebastiano del Piombo's Raising of Lazarus (1517 to 1519), painted with designs by Michelangelo in rivalry with Raphael, became the first painting catalogued by the National Gallery in London (NG1). Caravaggio's version (1609) is in Messina, Rembrandt's (about 1630 to 1632) is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and Vincent van Gogh, in the asylum at Saint-Rémy in 1890, painted part of Rembrandt's etching of the scene, giving Lazarus a red beard like his own. In literature, Søren Kierkegaard took the title of The Sickness unto Death (1849) from verse 4, arguing that the true sickness unto death is despair, and in Fyodor Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment (1866, part 4, chapter 4) Sonya reads this chapter aloud to the murderer Raskolnikov, the turning point of the novel.

Modern critical scholarship has debated the story's origin. David Friedrich Strauss (1835) treated it as myth; Rudolf Bultmann's commentary (1941) traced it to a source of miracle stories; others have suggested it grew from Jesus' parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31), which ends with the remark that people will not believe even if someone rises from the dead. John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 2, 1994) concluded that the story goes back to an event involving Lazarus that Jesus' disciples believed, during his lifetime, to be a raising from the dead. Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) suggested that the earlier Gospels left Lazarus out to protect him, since the chief priests planned to kill him too (12:10). The Secret Gospel of Mark, a text Morton Smith said he found at the monastery of Mar Saba and published in 1973, contains a Bethany raising story, but whether it is genuine is disputed, and Stephen Carlson (The Gospel Hoax, 2005) argued that Smith forged it.
text:
Only one manuscript difference in this chapter changes the sense noticeably. In verse 25 the early papyrus P45, one Old Latin manuscript, and the Sinaitic Syriac read only ‘I am the resurrection’, without ‘and the life’. Every other early witness, including P66, P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus, has the longer text, and all modern versions print it. In verse 50 the best manuscripts read ‘better for you’, where later manuscripts and the King James Version read ‘expedient for us’. In verse 31 the critical editions read that the mourners followed Mary ‘supposing’ she was going to the tomb; later manuscripts, and so the King James Version, read ‘saying’.

Other differences are translation. The King James Version renders verse 33 as ‘he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled’ and verse 38 as ‘groaning in himself’, where modern versions have ‘deeply moved’; neither fully captures the note of indignation in embrimaomai, and some versions add a note. Verse 39 is famous in the King James wording, ‘by this time he stinketh’. Verse 18 gives the distance as fifteen stadia, which versions render as about two miles or about three kilometers. Verse 35, ‘Jesus wept’, is the shortest verse in most English Bibles because of where the sixteenth-century verse divisions fell; in the Greek it is three words, and other verses are as short.

teach.big: Jesus, who weeps at the grave of his friend, is himself the resurrection and the life, and the sign that gives Lazarus life sets in motion the death by which Jesus will give life to the world.

outline.t: Jesus' love for this family is stated before his delay, so that the delay cannot be read as indifference; his purpose is the glory of God and a greater faith.
Jesus walks toward danger in the daylight of his Father's timing, and the disciples go with him, afraid and uncomprehending but loyal.
Jesus meets Martha's honest disappointment with a claim about himself: the resurrection is not only a future event but a present person.
Jesus meets Mary's grief with tears, showing that grief and faith are not enemies and that God is not distant from human sorrow.
At the word of Jesus the dead hear and come out, and the living are given the task of unbinding them.
The same sign produces faith in some and a plot in others, and God turns the plot into the means of salvation for many.
As Passover approaches, the hunted Jesus withdraws, but his hour is coming and the crowds wait to see what he will do.

teach.pitfalls:
The commonest misreading turns verse 35 into sentimentality, as if the point were only that Jesus had feelings. John pairs the tears with indignation (verses 33 and 38) and with the command at the tomb; the Jesus who weeps is also the one who will destroy death. A second misreading makes Martha the woman of little faith and Mary the woman of true devotion, borrowing a contrast from Luke 10:38-42. In John, Martha makes the chapter's great confession (verse 27), and both sisters speak the same honest words.

A third pitfall promises listeners that if they believe enough, God will raise or heal the person they love. The chapter's sign is unique, Lazarus later died again, and the promise of verses 25 and 26 is about the life Jesus gives now and the resurrection to come, not a guarantee of present rescue. A fourth uses the delay of verse 6 to tell grieving people that God is teaching them a lesson. Jesus did have a purpose in the delay, but he did not lecture the sisters about it; he came and wept with them. A fifth reads the council's plot as a Jewish plot against Jesus, when the chapter reports that many of the Jews believed (verse 45) and that the decision was made by a small group of leaders anxious about Rome. Finally, the chapter is not a detached argument for miracles; its aim is Martha's question to every reader: do you believe this?
teach.pastoral: This chapter will be heard by people who are grieving, some freshly, some for years, and some who prayed for someone who died anyway. They will hear the sisters' words, if you had been here, as their own. Teach that Jesus did not rebuke that sentence, that he wept, and that Christian hope does not require pretending the loss is small. Avoid implying that every death will be reversed now or that a lack of healing is a failure of faith. People who have lost someone to suicide or sudden death may hear the four days and the smell of the tomb with particular pain; speak of death honestly but without dwelling on its details. For some, the chapter may raise their own despair; Kierkegaard's reading of verse 4 is a reminder that the text speaks to the living dead as well as the grieving, and a teacher should know where to point anyone who needs more help than a sermon can give.

hard.q: If this was Jesus' greatest miracle, why do Matthew, Mark, and Luke never mention it, and did it happen?
hard.a:
The objection is serious. In John the raising of Lazarus is the public event that leads directly to Jesus' death (verses 47 to 53), yet the other three Gospels, which all tell of Jesus' last week in and around Jerusalem and of a supper at Bethany, never mention it and give a different trigger for the arrest, the incident in the temple. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) argued that the silence of the earlier Gospels shows the story to be a late legend built from Old Testament raisings and Jewish hope. Rudolf Bultmann (1941) traced it to a collection of miracle stories that John reworked. Several critical scholars have suggested that the story grew out of Luke's parable of a poor man named Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31), which ends with the warning that people will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead. Beneath these lies the general skeptical case, made classically by David Hume (1748), that no testimony can establish a miracle.

There are several responses. Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) argued that the earlier Gospels, circulating while the Jerusalem authorities still had power, left Lazarus out for his protection, since John 12:10 says the chief priests planned to kill him too, and that John, writing later, could name him. Others point out that the Synoptic Gospels focus on Galilee until the last week and omit much that John includes, and that they do record other raisings (Mark 5:21-43, Luke 7:11-17), so that belief in Jesus as one who raised the dead was not unique to John. John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 2, 1994), a cautious historian who does not claim to prove miracles, concluded that the story goes back to an event involving Lazarus that Jesus' disciples believed during his lifetime to be a raising from the dead. Many interpreters note the story's concrete details, the names, the village, the distance from Jerusalem, and the family known from Luke 10, and argue that John presents it as history. On the general question, whether such an event could happen depends on one's prior beliefs about God and nature, and historians who do not share the church's confession will weigh the report differently. The church confesses that the one who raised Lazarus was himself raised, and that confession, not this single event, is the ground of Christian hope.

hard.q: If Jesus loved Lazarus, why did he wait two days while his friend died?
hard.a:
The text puts the two facts together deliberately: “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So on hearing that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two days” (verses 5 and 6). The strongest form of the objection, pressed by skeptical readers and felt by many believers, is that love that could prevent grief and chooses not to is hard to call love, and that any purpose served by the sisters' anguish, even the glory of God, seems to use them as means to an end. Both sisters voice the complaint themselves (verses 21 and 32), and some bystanders put it sharply: could not this man have kept Lazarus from dying (verse 37)?

Interpreters answer in several ways. Some, following Calvin, stress that the delay was not indifference but purpose: Jesus says the sickness is for the glory of God (verse 4) and that he is glad for the disciples' sake that he was not there, so that they may believe (verse 15). He intended something greater than a healing, a raising that would show him as the resurrection and the life. Others note that Lazarus was probably already dead when the messengers arrived: a day for the message, two days' wait, and a day's travel add up to the four days of verse 17, so the delay may have changed nothing for Lazarus while making the sign unmistakable. Still others emphasize that in John Jesus acts only at his Father's time and never at human prompting (2:4, 7:6-10), so that the delay belongs to his obedience rather than to his feelings.

The hard part remains: the sisters suffered real grief, and both said so. Jesus doesn't rebuke them for it. He weeps with them. The chapter doesn't promise that God's love will always act on our schedule, and it does not explain every delay. What it shows is that his delays are not absence, and that he grieves in the meantime with those who are grieving.

observe: What does the sisters' message in verse 3 say, and what does it leave unsaid?
How does Jesus respond differently to Martha (verses 20 to 27) and to Mary (verses 28 to 35), even though they say the same words to him?
What reasons do the chief priests and Pharisees give in verses 47 and 48 for wanting to stop Jesus, and how does John interpret Caiaphas's reply?
interpret: What does Jesus mean when he says that whoever believes in him will live even though he dies, and that whoever lives and believes will never die?
Why do you think Jesus weeps and is deeply moved when he already knows he will raise Lazarus?
How does the raising of Lazarus lead to Jesus' own death, and why does John want us to see that connection?
apply: Martha and Mary both say, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” What would it look like to bring that kind of honest disappointment to Jesus?
Jesus asks Martha, “Do you believe this?” What difference does belief in the resurrection make to how you face your own death or the death of someone you love?
Jesus told others to unbind Lazarus. Who around you has been given new life but still needs help to be set free, and how might you help?
